claim: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) is hypothesized to play a central role in neural processes that regulate self-control.
source: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) is hypothesized to play a central role in neural processes that regulate self-control.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a hypothesis being tested in the study.

claim: At the single-neuron and population levels, STN shows a cost–benefit integration between the desirability of the expected reward and the imposed delay to reward delivery.
source: At the single-neuron and population levels, we found a cost–benefit integration between the desirability of the expected reward and the imposed delay to reward delivery, with STN signals that dynamically combined both attributes of the reward to form a single integrated estimate of value.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on the experimental data collected.

claim: STN signals dynamically combine reward size and delay to form a single integrated estimate of value.
source: At the single-neuron and population levels, we found a cost–benefit integration between the desirability of the expected reward and the imposed delay to reward delivery, with STN signals that dynamically combined both attributes of the reward to form a single integrated estimate of value.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on the experimental data.

claim: Neural encoding of subjective value in STN evolved dynamically across the waiting period that intervened after instruction cue.
source: This neural encoding of subjective value evolved dynamically across the waiting period that intervened after instruction cue.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on the experimental data.

claim: The encoding of temporally discounted value was distributed inhomogeneously along the antero-posterior axis of the STN.
source: Moreover, this encoding was distributed inhomogeneously along the antero-posterior axis of the STN such that the most dorso-posterior-placed neurons represented the temporal discounted value most strongly.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on the experimental data.

claim: The most dorso-posterior-placed neurons in STN represented the temporal discounted value most strongly.
source: Moreover, this encoding was distributed inhomogeneously along the antero-posterior axis of the STN such that the most dorso-posterior-placed neurons represented the temporal discounted value most strongly.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on the experimental data.

claim: All animals, including humans, prefer to receive rewards sooner rather than later, a phenomenon known as temporal discounting.
source: All animals, including humans, prefer to receive rewards sooner rather than later, a phenomenon known as temporal discounting (Frederick et al., 2002; Loewenstein and Prelec, 1993; Mazur, 2001; Vanderveldt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: People with low discount rates tend to pursue their long-term goals patiently.
source: Accordingly, people with low discount rates tend to pursue their long-term goals patiently, whereas people with high discount rates often abandon their goals impulsively and move on (Janakiraman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: People with high discount rates often abandon their goals impulsively.
source: Accordingly, people with low discount rates tend to pursue their long-term goals patiently, whereas people with high discount rates often abandon their goals impulsively and move on (Janakiraman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The STN is thought to be crucial in inhibitory control by preventing impulsivity.
source: Because the subthalamic nucleus (STN) is thought to be crucial in inhibitory control by preventing impulsivity (Aron et al., 2016; Bonnevie and Zaghloul, 2019; Jahanshahi et al., 2015) and modulating the performance of reward-seeking actions (Baunez et al., 2007; Baunez and Robbins, 1997), we hypothesized that this structure could contribute to the maintenance of adaptive behaviors by dynamically computing the temporally discounted value.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The STN modulates the performance of reward-seeking actions.
source: Because the subthalamic nucleus (STN) is thought to be crucial in inhibitory control by preventing impulsivity (Aron et al., 2016; Bonnevie and Zaghloul, 2019; Jahanshahi et al., 2015) and modulating the performance of reward-seeking actions (Baunez et al., 2007; Baunez and Robbins, 1997), we hypothesized that this structure could contribute to the maintenance of adaptive behaviors by dynamically computing the temporally discounted value.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rejection rates were affected by both reward size and delay to reward in both monkeys.
source: Rejection rates were affected by both reward size (two-way ANOVAs; monkey H: F(2,666) = 10.47, p<0.001; monkey C: F(2,708) = 5.36, p=0.0049) and delay to reward (H: F(1,666) = 22.62, p<0.001; C: F(1,708) = 8.03, p=0.0047).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The proportion of rejected trials was higher for smaller rewards and longer delays.
source: The proportion of rejected trials was higher for smaller rewards and longer delays, while both animals waited more patiently to obtain larger rewards.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on behavioral data analysis.

claim: Interactive effects between reward size and delay revealed an integration of both task parameters to estimate the overall desirability or subjective value of each cost–benefit condition.
source: Interactive effects between reward size and delay (H: F(2,666) = 19.31, p<0.001; C: F(2,708) = 10.31, p<0.001) revealed an integration of both task parameters to estimate the overall desirability or subjective value of each cost–benefit condition.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The animals' task performance was well approximated by an inverse relation with hyperbolic delay discounting.
source: Consistent with other monkey studies (Hori et al., 2021; Minamimoto et al., 2009), the animals' task performance was well approximated by an inverse relation with hyperbolic delay discounting (H: R2 = 0.98; C: R2 = 0.86; Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on behavioral data analysis and model fitting, with reference to Figure 1D and E.

claim: Monkey C was more impatient with a steeper delay discounting (k = 1.62 s–1) compared to monkey H (k = 1.28 s–1).
source: In comparison, however, monkey C was a bit more impatient with a steeper delay discounting (k = 1.62 s–1), while the subjective value estimated by monkey H was slightly less impacted by the cost of waiting (k = 1.28 s–1).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on behavioral data analysis and model fitting.

claim: Muscle patterns were not altered by reward contingencies during the post-instruction waiting interval.
source: As evidenced by a series of two-way ANOVAs (reward × delay, p<0.05/173-time bins), muscle patterns were not altered by reward contingencies.
evidence: This is a control finding based on EMG data analysis.

claim: Eye position was affected by both the expected reward size and delay after the presentation of instruction cues.
source: Eye position was affected by both the expected reward size and delay after the presentation of instruction cues (two-way ANOVAs, p<0.05/173-time bins).
evidence: This is a control finding based on eye tracking data analysis.

claim: 231 neurons were recorded from the right STN (112 from monkey H; 119 from monkey C).
source: While the monkeys performed the delayed reward task, we recorded single-unit activity from 231 neurons in the right STN (112 from monkey H; 119 from monkey C).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collected.

claim: Approximately 42% of STN neurons demonstrated a peak in activity in the first second following presentation of the instruction cues.
source: Approximately 42% of neurons demonstrated a peak in activity in the first second following presentation of the instruction cues, while 32% of neurons exhibited highest discharge rates later during the waiting period (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on analysis of neuronal data, with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: 32% of STN neurons exhibited highest discharge rates later during the waiting period.
source: Approximately 42% of neurons demonstrated a peak in activity in the first second following presentation of the instruction cues, while 32% of neurons exhibited highest discharge rates later during the waiting period (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on analysis of neuronal data, with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: 112 neurons (48%) were modulated by reward size.
source: Of the 231 neurons recorded, 112 (48%; 21 from monkey H and 91 from monkey C) and 91 (39%; 18 from monkey H and 73 from monkey C) were modulated by reward size and delay, respectively (Figure 2G–J).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on statistical analysis of neuronal data, with reference to Figure 2G-J.

claim: 91 neurons (39%) were modulated by delay.
source: Of the 231 neurons recorded, 112 (48%; 21 from monkey H and 91 from monkey C) and 91 (39%; 18 from monkey H and 73 from monkey C) were modulated by reward size and delay, respectively (Figure 2G–J).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on statistical analysis of neuronal data, with reference to Figure 2G-J.

claim: Encoding of reward size occurred preferentially immediately following cue presentation.
source: Immediately following cue presentation, neurons were strongly influenced by the reward size signaled by the instruction while, later in the trial, as animals endured the waiting period, encoding of delay became more common.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on temporal analysis of neuronal data.

claim: Encoding of delay became more common later in the trial as animals endured the waiting period.
source: Immediately following cue presentation, neurons were strongly influenced by the reward size signaled by the instruction while, later in the trial, as animals endured the waiting period, encoding of delay became more common.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on temporal analysis of neuronal data.

claim: 79 neurons (34%) were sensitive to both reward size and delay at some point over the course of the trial.
source: Among the 79 neurons (34%; 14 from monkey H and 65 from monkey C) sensitive to both parameters at some point over the course of the trial, 50 (22%; 8 from monkey H and 42 from monkey C) were influenced simultaneously by reward size and delay within the same time bins, thereby reflecting a direct integration of cost–benefit conditions by individual neurons (Figure 2K and L).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on statistical analysis of neuronal data, with reference to Figure 2K and L.

claim: 50 neurons (22%) were influenced simultaneously by reward size and delay within the same time bins.
source: Among the 79 neurons (34%; 14 from monkey H and 65 from monkey C) sensitive to both parameters at some point over the course of the trial, 50 (22%; 8 from monkey H and 42 from monkey C) were influenced simultaneously by reward size and delay within the same time bins, thereby reflecting a direct integration of cost–benefit conditions by individual neurons (Figure 2K and L).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on statistical analysis of neuronal data, with reference to Figure 2K and L.

claim: Neural activities were often influenced in opposite directions by the predicted amount of reward and the delay.
source: Neural activities were often influenced in opposite directions by the predicted amount of reward and the delay (positive βReward with negative βDelay, or vice versa).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on regression analysis of neuronal data.

claim: During phase 1 (0-2 s post-instruction), the neural ensemble encoded information about reward size and delay in a pattern strongly consistent with temporal discounting of value (Discounting–).
source: Notably, the angle of the mean vector across all neurons (θ1 = –12°, Figure 4C) showed that, despite the wide diversity of encoding patterns across individual neurons in phase 1, the whole neural ensemble encoded information about reward size and delay in a pattern that was strongly consistent with a temporal discounting of value (i.e., Discounting–).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on population-level analysis of neuronal data, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: In phase 1, 60 neurons (48%) increased firing rates as a function of reward size while they decreased according to the temporal delay to reward delivery (Discounting– pattern).
source: Of the 124 task-related neurons, 60 (48%) increased firing rates as a function of reward size while they decreased according to the temporal delay to reward delivery (i.e., consistent with a Discounting– pattern).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on categorization of neuronal encoding patterns.

claim: In phase 2 (2-3.5 s post-instruction), the population encoding changed drastically to a predominantly Compounding pattern.
source: Then, in phase 2, the population encoding of reward size and delay parameters changed drastically to a predominantly Compounding pattern (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on population-level analysis of neuronal data, with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: In phase 2, 42 neurons (34%) increased firing rates as a function of both reward size and delay (Compounding+ pattern).
source: Of the 124 task-related neurons, 42 (34%) increased firing rates during this period as a function of both reward size and delay (i.e., consistent with a Compounding+ pattern), while only 24 (19%) were still categorized as Discounting– type neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on categorization of neuronal encoding patterns.

claim: 27 individual units (22%) switched encoding pattern from Discounting– to Compounding+ in the transition from phase 1 to phase 2.
source: This dynamic shift in the encoding of task-relevant information (i.e., rotation of the vectors between phases 1 and 2) was detected not only at the population level but also in the activities of 27 individual units (22%) in which the encoding pattern switched from Discounting– to Compounding+ in the transition from phase 1 to phase 2, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on analysis of individual neuronal encoding patterns over time.

claim: Neurons categorized as Discounting– in phase 1 and/or Compounding+ in phase 2 were located preferentially in the most posterior and dorsal portion of the STN.
source: Remarkably, the neurons categorized as Discounting– in phase 1 and/or Compounding+ in phase 2 were located preferentially in the most posterior and dorsal portion of the STN (two-sample t-test, t(229) > 3.04, p<0.05; Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on anatomical analysis of neuronal locations, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: Discounting– neurons and Compounding+ neurons did not differ from other types of STN neurons with respect to tonic firing rate or action potential shape.
source: Discounting– neurons (Figure 5A–G) and Compounding+ neurons (Figure 5H–N) did not differ from other types of STN neurons with respect to tonic firing rate (t(229) < 1.87, p>0.06) or action potential shape (t(229) < 1.03, p>0.3).
evidence: This is a control finding based on statistical comparison of neuronal properties, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: The first four principal components (PCs) from the real data exceeded the 95% confidence interval of variances accounted for by PCs from the surrogate control PCAs.
source: We found that the first four PCs from the real data exceeded the 95% confidence interval of variances accounted for by PCs from the surrogate control PCAs.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on PCA analysis with statistical validation.

claim: The first four PCs explained 72.4% of the total variance.
source: In total, the first four PCs explained 72.4% of the total variance (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on PCA analysis, with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: PC1 accounted for 45.1% of variance and corresponded primarily to a temporal discounting of reward value that later evolved to a Compounding+ pattern.
source: Consistent with our single-unit analyses, the first principal component (PC1, which accounted for 45.1% of variance) corresponded primarily to a temporal discounting of reward value (i.e., a signal that increased with increasing reward size and decreased with increasing delay; –90° < θ < 0°) that later evolved to a Compounding+ pattern (i.e., a signal in which reward size and delay were integrated in an additive manner; 0° < θ < 90°).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on PCA analysis of population-level neuronal data.

claim: PC2 accounted for 13.9% of variance and showed a transient encoding of reward size only in the first second after instruction, then deviated to a robust Discounting+ pattern.
source: The signal captured by PC2 (second column of Figure 6; accounting for 13.9% of variance) differed markedly from that of PC1. In the 1 s after presentation of the instruction cue, the PC2 population signal was primarily sensitive to reward size only, with a transient encoding pointing toward 0°. Then, approximately 2 s after the instruction, PC2 deviated to a robust Discounting+ pattern (90° < θ < 180°) in which reward size and delay had opposing effects on the signal.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on PCA analysis of population-level neuronal data, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: PC3 accounted for 7.4% of total variance and revealed a population signal with two consecutive temporal phases.
source: Similarly, the eigenvector properties for PC3 (7.4% of total variance explained; third column of Figure 6) revealed a population signal that involved two consecutive temporal phases.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on PCA analysis of population-level neuronal data, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: PC4 accounted for 6% of variance and was characterized by multiple salient signals reflecting reward values only and Discounting+ patterns.
source: Finally, the signal extracted by PC4 (6% of variance explained) was characterized by multiple salient signals reflecting reward values only (close to 0°) and Discounting+ (90° < θ < 180°) during relatively short periods after instruction.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on PCA analysis of population-level neuronal data.

claim: Component scores for PC1 correlated significantly with neuronal position along the ventro-anterior to dorso-posterior axis in the STN (Spearman's rho = 0.35, p<0.001).
source: Because the scores for PC1 (Spearman's rho = 0.35, p<0.001; Figure 7) and PC2 (rho = 0.19, p=0.003) increased along the ventro-anterior to dorso-posterior axis in the STN, this result indicates that reward size and delay were integrated into a common value most strongly in the dorso-posterior STN.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on correlation analysis of PC scores with anatomical location, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: Component scores for PC2 correlated significantly with neuronal position along the ventro-anterior to dorso-posterior axis in the STN (Spearman's rho = 0.19, p=0.003).
source: Because the scores for PC1 (Spearman's rho = 0.35, p<0.001; Figure 7) and PC2 (rho = 0.19, p=0.003) increased along the ventro-anterior to dorso-posterior axis in the STN, this result indicates that reward size and delay were integrated into a common value most strongly in the dorso-posterior STN.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on correlation analysis of PC scores with anatomical location, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: Reward size and delay were integrated into a common value most strongly in the dorso-posterior STN.
source: Because the scores for PC1 (Spearman's rho = 0.35, p<0.001; Figure 7) and PC2 (rho = 0.19, p=0.003) increased along the ventro-anterior to dorso-posterior axis in the STN, this result indicates that reward size and delay were integrated into a common value most strongly in the dorso-posterior STN.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation analysis results, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: No significant correlations were found in the spatial distribution of PC3 and PC4 scores.
source: No significant correlations were found in the spatial distribution of PC3 and PC4 scores (rho < 0.08, p>0.21), suggesting that these population signals were processed by neurons anatomically intermixed with others in the entire STN.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on correlation analysis of PC scores with anatomical location.

claim: The STN occupies a unique position for translating motivational drives into behavioral perseverance, standing at the crossroads between the basal ganglia indirect pathway and many hyperdirect inputs from prefrontal areas.
source: The STN occupies a unique position for translating motivational drives into behavioral perseverance, standing at the crossroads between the basal ganglia indirect pathway and many hyperdirect inputs from prefrontal areas involved in motivational, cognitive and motor functions (Haynes and Haber, 2013; Parent and Hazrati, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical research.

claim: Increased activity in the STN extends the time to action initiation by elevating decision thresholds, preventing suboptimal early responses or decisions.
source: Current functional models of the STN propose that increased activity in the STN extends the time to action initiation by elevating decision thresholds, preventing suboptimal early responses or decisions, especially in situations in which the motivational options are conflicting (Cavanagh et al., 2011; Frank, 2006; Mansfield et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical and modeling research.

claim: Lesion studies on rats provided causal evidence that STN restrains premature responding in instrumental tasks.
source: In support of these models, a series of lesion studies performed on rats provided causal evidence that STN restrains premature responding in instrumental tasks (Baunez and Robbins, 1997; Wiener et al., 2008) and controls the willingness to work for food (Baunez et al., 2005; Baunez et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior lesion studies.

claim: Dysfunctions of STN circuits produced perseverative actions with a reduced ability to switch between behaviors.
source: Dysfunctions of STN circuits even produced perseverative actions with a reduced ability to switch between behaviors (Baker and Ragozzino, 2014; Baunez et al., 2007), making this brain region a good candidate for regulating self-control and delayed gratification.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Deep brain stimulation of STN (DBS-STN) may induce side effects related to altered motivation such as depression, excessive eating behavior, and hypomania.
source: In particular, deep brain stimulation (DBS-STN), which is effective at alleviating motor symptoms in parkinsonian patients, may induce a variety of side effects related to altered motivation such as depression, excessive eating behavior, and hypomania (Berney et al., 2002; Castrioto et al., 2014; Jahanshahi et al., 2015; Voon et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical research.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings from the STN of parkinsonian patients have shown low-frequency oscillations (<12 Hz) and spiking activities related to various aspects of reward processing.
source: Electrophysiological recordings collected from the STN of these patients have shown low-frequency oscillations (<12 Hz) and spiking activities related to various aspects of reward processing, with neural signals modulated by the magnitude of monetary reward and cost–benefit value attribution (Fumagalli et al., 2015; Justin Rossi et al., 2017; Zénon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior human electrophysiology research.

claim: STN neurons fire as a function of the expected reward and the associated effort cost.
source: In non-human animals, the ability of the STN to represent the subjective desirability of actions has also been evidenced by studies that show neurons firing as a function of the expected reward and the associated effort cost (Breysse et al., 2015; Espinosa-Parrilla et al., 2013; Nougaret et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior animal electrophysiology research.

claim: The STN is organized into anatomically and functionally distinct territories.
source: In addition, it is still unclear how these roles for STN in cost–benefit valuation and motivational processing relate to the known organization of this nucleus into anatomically and functionally distinct territories (Alexander et al., 1990; Nambu et al., 2002; Parent and Hazrati, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical research.

claim: Monkeys selected the more advantageous option in terms of reward when delays were equal (H: 97%, C: 99%).
source: Monkeys selected the more advantageous option in terms of reward when the delays were equal (H: 97%, t(14) = 26.99, p<0.001; C: 99%, t(16) = 30.55, p<0.001) and the more advantageous delay option when reward sizes were held constant (H: 99%, t(11) = 29.71, p<0.001; C: 95%, t(10) = 24.82, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a control finding based on behavioral data from the decision task.

claim: Monkeys selected the more advantageous delay option when reward sizes were held constant (H: 99%, C: 95%).
source: Monkeys selected the more advantageous option in terms of reward when the delays were equal (H: 97%, t(14) = 26.99, p<0.001; C: 99%, t(16) = 30.55, p<0.001) and the more advantageous delay option when reward sizes were held constant (H: 99%, t(11) = 29.71, p<0.001; C: 95%, t(10) = 24.82, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a control finding based on behavioral data from the decision task.

claim: The tripartite model divides STN into segregated motor, associative, and limbic regions.
source: Based on this, a widely accepted tripartite model divides STN into segregated motor, associative, and limbic regions that are thought to play distinct roles in motor control, cognition, and emotion (Parent and Hazrati, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior anatomical research.

claim: In previous primate studies, reward-responsive neurons were found to be scattered throughout all parts of the STN.
source: Surprisingly, in previous primate studies, reward-responsive neurons were found to be scattered throughout all parts of the STN (Darbaky et al., 2005; Espinosa-Parrilla et al., 2013; Nougaret et al., 2022), rather than showing a preferential location in the anterior portion that is held to be the zone with strongest connectivity to limbic structures (Haynes and Haber, 2013; Karachi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior primate electrophysiology research.

claim: Reward-modulated neurons were identified in sensorimotor regions of the STN in human recordings.
source: That lack of anatomic specificity has been confirmed in human recordings for which reward-modulated neurons were also identified in sensorimotor regions of the STN (Justin Rossi et al., 2017; Sieger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior human electrophysiology research.

claim: The present results challenge predictions from the classical tripartite model of STN functional topography.
source: At the single-neuron and population levels (Figures 5 and 7), we found that the valuation of delayed rewards was represented preferentially in the most dorso-posterior portion of the STN, thereby challenging predictions from the classical tripartite model of STN functional topography.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the anatomical findings in relation to existing models, with reference to Figures 5 and 7.

claim: Recent evidence points toward overlapping territories in STN rather than segregated functional subdivisions.
source: While earlier studies suggested segregated functional subdivisions, now more recent evidence points toward overlapping territories (Alkemade and Forstmann, 2014; Emmi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: Patients with self-control issues such as gambling disorder, drug addiction, schizophrenia, depression, mania, ADHD, and anxiety disorder have higher delay discounting rates than normal subjects.
source: For instance, patients with self-control issues such as in gambling disorder (Alessi and Petry, 2003), drug addiction (Kirby and Petry, 2004; Madden et al., 1997; Washio et al., 2011), schizophrenia (Ahn et al., 2011; Heerey et al., 2007; MacKillop and Tidey, 2011), depression (Dombrovski et al., 2012; Pulcu et al., 2014; Takahashi et al., 2008), mania (Mason et al., 2012), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (Barkley et al., 2001; Scheres et al., 2010; Tripp and Alsop, 2001), and anxiety disorder Rounds et al., 2007 have higher delay discounting rates than normal subjects.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior clinical research.

claim: DBS-STN has beneficial effects on drug addiction in animal studies.
source: This view agrees with the beneficial effects of DBS-STN on drug addiction reported in recent animal studies (Pelloux et al., 2018; Rouaud et al., 2010; Wade et al., 2017), and with the battery of psychiatric side effects observed in parkinsonian patients after electrode implantation within the STN (Castrioto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior animal research.

claim: Psychiatric side effects are observed in parkinsonian patients after electrode implantation within the STN.
source: This view agrees with the beneficial effects of DBS-STN on drug addiction reported in recent animal studies (Pelloux et al., 2018; Rouaud et al., 2010; Wade et al., 2017), and with the battery of psychiatric side effects observed in parkinsonian patients after electrode implantation within the STN (Castrioto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior clinical research.

claim: Two rhesus monkeys (monkey C, 8 kg, male; and monkey H, 6 kg, female) were used in this study.
source: Two rhesus monkeys (monkey C, 8 kg, male; and monkey H, 6 kg, female) were used in this study.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the University of Pittsburgh (protocol number: 12111162).
source: Procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the University of Pittsburgh (protocol number: 12111162) and complied with the Public Health Service Policy on the humane care and use of laboratory animals (amended 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: The hyperbolic discounting model has been shown to fit monkey behavior better than an exponential function.
source: In previous studies (Hori et al., 2021; Kobayashi and Schultz, 2008; Minamimoto et al., 2009), this hyperbolic discounting model has been shown consistently to fit to monkey behavior better than an exponential function.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The Fano factor showed that task-relevant information was processed by STN neurons not only immediately after instruction cue presentation, but also later during the post-instruction delay period.
source: Despite the fact that phasic changes evoked by instruction cues dominated the population-averaged activity (Figure 2E), we found that the variability of neuronal activities across the six reward/delay conditions was maintained at an elevated constant level across several seconds of the trial, as evidenced by the Fano Factor shown in Figure 2F. This suggests that task-relevant information was processed by STN neurons not only immediately after the presentation of the instruction cue, but also later in the course of the post-instruction delay period, when the animal was maintaining a stable arm position in anticipation of reward delivery.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Fano factor analysis, with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: The way STN neurons represented task conditions evolved dynamically across the course of a trial.
source: Overall, these results suggest that the way STN neurons represented task conditions evolved dynamically across the course of a trial.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the temporal analysis of neuronal data.

claim: Temporal discounting likely originates from different neural circuits than those that signal expected reward value.
source: The fact we were able to dissociate in the STN these two types of neurons suggests that temporal discounting originates likely from different neural circuits than those that signal expected reward value.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of distinct neuronal populations encoding reward size versus delay.

claim: Dynamic value integration through the STN may regulate the expression of persistent behaviors for which a continuously evolving cost–benefit estimation is required.
source: Such dynamic value integration through the STN may regulate the expression of persistent behaviors for which a continuously evolving cost–benefit estimation is required to monitor and sustain goal achievement.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings in the context of behavioral regulation.

claim: Motivational signals in STN were conveyed by neurons located in areas traditionally identified as part of the sensorimotor circuits.
source: Consistent with a functional convergence within this structure, our results show that motivational signals were conveyed by neurons located in areas traditionally identified as part of the sensorimotor circuits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the anatomical findings in relation to traditional functional subdivisions.

claim: The role of STN in self-control extends understanding concerning its involvement in the control of impulsive behaviors and the willingness to work for food.
source: This role in self-control extends our understanding concerning the involvement of STN in the control of impulsive behaviors (Aron et al., 2016; Jahanshahi et al., 2015; Zavala et al., 2015) and the willingness to work for food (Baunez et al., 2005; Baunez et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to prior research, supported by citations.

claim: STN promotes the pursuit of motivated behavior by computing which costs are acceptable for the reward at stake.
source: By providing evidence for dynamic cost–benefit valuation by STN, our results imply that this structure promotes the pursuit of motivated behavior by computing which costs are acceptable for the reward at stake.
evidence: This is an interpretation and implication of the findings.

claim: The STN may be a potential hub to regulate aberrant reward processing and the capability to postpone in psychiatric disorders.
source: Our results merge existing lines of evidence that implicate the STN in motivation and inhibitory control, positioning this structure as a potential hub to regulate aberrant reward processing and the capability to postpone.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings in the context of clinical applications.
